content.text: The evidence is clear: no deployments/config changes, error spike caused by `PaymentProviderFailed: api.io-pay.example returned 503`, and io-pay is a third-party dependency owned by IO Payments Ltd.

hypotheses.subject: api.io-pay.example
hypotheses.summary: io-shop's account page began failing because its third-party card/payment dependency, api.io-pay.example (io-pay), started returning 503 errors on every card lookup call. No deployment, config, or flag change occurred on io-shop in the preceding day, and cpu/memory/traffic stayed flat through the incident, so the fault originates entirely upstream in io-pay.

supporting_evidence.claim: ERROR io-shop: account page request failed - PaymentProviderFailed: api.io-pay.example returned 503 for /v1/shoppers/shopper-64320-11-0/card at src/io_shop/payment_provider.py:95
WARN io-shop: account page error rate at 100.00% over the last minute
io-pay: third-party, owned by IO Payments Ltd, at api.io-pay.example - Holds the card Io charges. Called while the account page renders
cpu_used_cores and cpu_limit_cores held steady at ~0.7-0.79 / 3.0 through onset, and request_volume stayed at 1200 across the whole window including the incident minutes

hypotheses.summary: If io-pay were instead an internally-owned dependency this would be classed as internal-dependency-failure, but the service register explicitly marks it third-party/IO Payments Ltd, so this is ruled out in favor of the upstream-dependency hypothesis above.
